speakeroldname: Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue):
maintopic: GASOLINE PRICES
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) asked me a question and was good enough to furnish me with the newspaper clipping upon which the question was based. The question related to gasoline, and this newspaper item has the caption:
The Joker in the Gasoline Tariff
If it is a joker, Mr. Speaker, it is a joker that has been there from 1904, more definitely from 1907, and down to the present time. I am told that the provision in the customs tariff upon which the only allegation of a joker could be made was inserted in the tariff by the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. The newspaper article goes on to say:
The Canadian government has been praised for removing the dumping duty on gasoline. But dispatches which intimated that all artificial valuation of this product for duty purposes was to be abandoned were astray.
I think that word " artificial " should read "real," because it deals with the fair market value of the goods for home consumption, as provided for by Mr. Fielding. That value of course included the excise tax. I think where there is an excise tax in the home market it must be obvious that that must be taken into consideration in arriving at the fair market value for any purpose whatever. If any one doubts that, let me say that the statute expressly provides that the excise tax of any foreign country in relation to the market value shall be taken into consideration

Gasoline Prices
if that country is under the general tariff. Therefore in this case the excise tax of the United States of one cent a gallon must apply. There is no escape from it. It has been the law for a long time and it is the law today.
A bulletin from Ottawa says that the Canadian importer must bring in his gasoline at the price for home consumption in the United States.
That is the law.
That is. he must import it at a price which includes the United States excise tax of a cent a gallon-slightly more than a cent on the Canadian gallon-although the United States government does not levy this tax at all on gasoline for export.
But we are not talking about gasoline for export, we are talking about gasoline and its value in the home market, what it sells for there. Of course the United States gives certain benefits to its exporters, as we do in our customs tariff:
The Canadian government imposes this United States tax.
There is nothing but an untruth in that statement, Mr. Speaker. Of course Canada does not impose any United States tax.
But the Canadian government does not get it. The United States manufacturer puts it in his pocket. His own government does not take it from him because he is exporting the gasoline. But he must, by order of Canada,-
How unfair and untrue that statement is!
-invoice the gasoline at a price w-hich includes it. So by order of the Canadian government the American manufacturer gets an extra cent.
The Canadian government does not deal with gasoline in any manner other than that in which it deals with any other articles that are brought in from the United States. This appraiser's bulletin which is referred to contains, as I have hastily summed them up, over twenty-five items, and gasoline appears in about the centre of these items, and they are all treated in the same way. So that if there is any inference that gasoline is subject to any other charge or import than relates to other articles in the same class or the same category, it is wholly untrue. And this bulletin was issued in the routine of the department in order to inform the collectors of customs specifically what under the law they should do. Instructions given and instructions expected to be followed. I am sorry to have had to labour this matter, but this article goes on to say:
The Canadian importer must not only pay this extra cent per American gallon but he must pay the exchange on it, and pay also the sales and excise taxes on the extra cent and on the exchange.
The inference there is that gasoline is subject to special taxes which are not levied in other cases. There is no hon. member of this house who does not know that this inference is untrue; in all similar cases the sales and excise taxes are levied and collected. The article goes on:
It amounts, when all is totalled up and allowance made for the difference in the American and Canadian gallon, to a cent and a half per gallon extra which the Canadian consumer has to pay because of the ruling from Ottawa that gasoline must be imported at the price for home consumption in the United States.
I have explained, Mr. Speaker, that there is no ruling from Ottawa. There is a statute of this country, which was initially placed upon the statute books by Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. The article concludes:
Under this absurd arrangement-[DOT]
Which is statutory.
-one cent of the additional impost goes to the American manufacturer and about half a cent to the Canadian government, in addition, of course, to the duty of two and a half cents per imperial gallon.
How that half cent is worked out in favour of the Canadian government I do not understand, unless it has to do with the sales tax, the special excise tax and the exchange situation, all of which apply to other cases dealt with in a similar way. Gasoline is not an exception. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this article has a line of untruth and misrepresentation running right through it. If anyone wants to know what is the duty on gasoline today, I may say that it is the duty which has been determined by parliament, two and a half cents per imperial gallon.

maintopic: GASOLINE PRICES

I would say that no such fixation was made. We did determine, as fairly and accurately as could be done, what was the fair market value of gasoline at certain pivotal points in the United States. I believed that was a fair thing to do, but it was the desire of many that it should not be done, and as a consequence that practice has ceased, as I believe my hon. friend knows. Now that we are simply carrying out the law I presume no objection can be raised by my hon. friend from Willow Bunch or by any other hon. member of this house.

Last night, Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned we were discussing the question of the shipment of wheat via American ports. It will be recalled that the question has been raised a number of times in the house, and the Prime Minister has read the British regulations in regard to such ship-
[Mr. Ryekman.l
ments. Undoubtedly if those regulations are to be interpreted literally it will be impossible for Canadian wheat to get the preference if it goes via United States ports. In reading the regulations the Prime Minister did not himself undertake to interpret them; if I am not mistaken he simply read them and left it to us to put our own interpretation upon them. In my mind there is no question that if the regulations are to be interpreted literally wheat shipped via United States ports can have no expectation of getting the preference.
In discussing the matter with some of my colleagues, however, we felt that perhaps some arrangement might be arrived at if the regulations were interpreted liberally, which has been indicated as the intention in regard to all these agreements. Suspicions have developed in our minds that there is a definite arrangement in this connection which is part of a definite plan to divert Canadian wheat from the United States to the Canadian route.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
That is the situation, and I want to know if that is true. Some grounds for that suspicion-we will not call it anything stronger at the moment-have been found in a statement recently made in the British house. I should like to quote a brief extract from an article appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press, which contains a Canadian Press report from England:
When an amendment was moved to allow the reconsignment of Canadian wheat in the United States, if the identity were certified by a Canadian government official, a statement was made by Leslie Hore-Belisha, financial secretary of the treasury. The Canadian Press reports says:
"Mr. Hore-Belisha explained the government had two reasons for refusing the amendment. Firstly, he said, customs procedure would make it extremely difficult to identify the wheat, and secondly, it would be against established policy.
"The government, he continued, had always made it a matter of policy to insist goods which enjoyed preferential tariff treatment in the United Kingdom be consigned from an empire country as well as have origin there.
"The purpose of the decision against reconsignment of Canadian wheat from the United States, he explained, was 'to encourage_ the storage of wheat either in Canada, which is to obtain the preference, or in the United Kingdom where we may obtain the advantage of storage and warehouse dues.' "
Mr. Hore-Belisha ended by asking: "Is not Canada in a position to store wheat and is not the United Kingdom in a position to store wheat?"
This has given rise to the suspicion in our minds that some understanding, some definite arrangement has been arrived at between the Canadian delegates and the British delegates, whereby such a strict interpretation shall be put upon the British regidation. If we are

United Kingdom
mistaken in that regard, we shall be very glad to hear it. I have no complaint to make against the British government; no doubt they have a right to fix any regulations they please with respect to the importation of wheat. \\ hat we should like to know, however, is what attitude has ibeen taken by our government in the matter. Has an understanding been arrived at? Have any suggestions been made in all the negotiations that have taken place between our delegates and the British delegates that such action should be taken, or has it been intimated to the British delegates that that rigid construction placed upon the regulations would be acceptable to the Canadian delegates?

speechtext:
I was going to observe that this matter is one within the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom alone, and any regulations which they may desire to make restricting or extending in any way the conditions under which the preference on empire goods may be extended to goods imported into the United Kingdom is their problem, within their jurisdiction, and for their consideration and decision alone. Similarly, the conditions under which goods of empire origin may be imported into this country and receive the preference are wholly within the jurisdiction of this parliament and have, I think, been well settled by this parliament. If there is one thing for which I can give credit to the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition it is that he made that a fixed principle so far as * importations of Canadian goods under the British preference are concerned. In that he had our support.
Now, this is a question which is agitating the minds of our people in eastern Canada. For years our people down there have been putting up a fight and appealing to their brethren in western Canada to do something for empire trade through eastern Canadian ports. I may observe to my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, who is smiling, that this matter is equally important to his port.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am
agreeing with you.

When the government of the United Kingdom, under the regulations passed in connection with the Import Duties Act of 1932, passed regulation No. 12, so far as Canada is concerned, I apprehend that they settled the question for themselves and that it will be the duty as well as the privilege of shippers of Canadian products such as wheat and other commodities

to conform to their regulations if they want the preference, and it is none of the business of this government what the United Kingdom government has done in that regard. It just so happens that a proper interpretation of regulation 12 will promote that for which we in the Atlantic ports of Canada have been standing for and striving for for years. The facilities in connection with our ports can be used under this regulation, provided always there is sufficient storage on the seaboard to take advantage of the situation which has been created under the jurisdiction of the United Kingdom, and I want to appeal to our friends from western Canada, to help work out these regulations and the exportation of goods of Canadian origin through Canadian ports in the spirit in which it was intended by the British government that they should be worked out.
What is the position? It is this, as I apprehend it. There is no interruption in the shipment of Canadian wheat through American ports, provided always that it is consigned from the country of origin. to the importing country on a through bill of lading.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It can't be done.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: To say that it has never been done is not to say that it cannot be done. To take the position that you are never to do something simply because it has never been done is absurd.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It is not practicable.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I say it
is practicable, "and I intend to show that it is practicable to any reasonable mind -and in that I desire for the moment to include the hon. member for Weyburn. I am trying to approach the subject, not in any narrow political partisan spirit at all, but from the point of view of a representative of eastern Canada who is vitally interested in the question. After all, as I have pointed out on many occasions, the people of St. John, out of their own pockets, tried for many years to build up this export business, and I am sorry to say that they got very little support from western Canada. It has been a tedious process of education and in many instances a most disappointing process because the results have not proved to be what our people have naturally looked for and what they say as a part and parcel of confederation they have a right to expect. I am not one who believes that you can alter the channels of commerce by a single stroke of the pen; I know that it is difficult to change the routes of commerce but when an

opportunity arises to change those routes without detriment to those who are immediately interested, then I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite and particularly to hon. members from western Canada to give this matter a fair trial before condemning it offhand. The situation with respect to through consignments on through bills of lading has not been altered.
My colleague reminds me that hon. members have the Hudson Bay railway, but I shall leave that out of this discussion. I am trying to rivet the attention of the house and the country upon what is of substantial importance to the people with whom I am associated in the east, that is, the use of our ports for the shipment of Canadian products. So far as I have been able to understand the regulations, the only change I can see that has been made is that it will be no longer possible for shippers of Canadian wheat to store their grain at Buffalo. This storage has been carried on for years and I understand that very extensive commitments have been made in the way of storage facilities. It will be no longer possible for them to carry on in that way because they would not be able to ship on a through bill of lading from storage at Buffalo. From our point of view this is all to the good, although I expect hon. friends opposite to disagree. They have a right to their own opinion, but I say to them that had these commitments for storage facilities been made on the Canadian side, as I think they should have been made, there would have been no difficulty presenting itself at this moment. Furthermore, I understand that both the great railway systems of this country have put into effect a rate from the lower lake ports such as Midland, Port Colborne, Port McNicoll and elsewhere, where storage facilities are available, to our eastern ports equal to the rate from Buffalo to New York.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The hon. member is mistaken.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I do not think I am wrong. As a matter of fact, no hon. member can say that this is or is not so without producing the rates in question. First class evidence of that character cannot be produced but I am informed by those who say they know that the railways not only have agreed to establish but have established this rate. Proceeding on the assumption that a six-cent rate has been established to Saint John and Halifax, and without considering whether or not that is an adequate rate, I say that there is no longer any excuse for the western shipper to continue to ship through

United Kingdom
New York at the expense of Canadian ports. What is the excuse offered? It is that tonnage may not be available. I do not pretend to be an expert in grain matters-a number of hon. gentlemen opposite do pretend to be experts, but on many occasions I have had my doubts-but I recognize that it is important that tonnage should be available. The chairman of the Halifax harbour commission who has made a very intensive study of this subject has told me that the availability of tonnage will not retard the movement of this commodity because if, as and when it is required, it will be obtainable. If he is correct in his statement the last point of opposition to this routing of Canadian wheat and other goods of Canadian origin is wiped out.
My appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite and to the public of western Canada is to give this matter a fair trial. I ask them not to bring pressure upon this government or upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce to have the British government change its regulations. If they do, I warn them here and now that there will be opposition to this move by the people of the maritime provinces. I put this proposal, which I think is a fair one, to hon. gentlemen opposite: give these provisions, established by a competent jurisdiction, the British government, a fair trial and then if you find you are being penalized, it will be time enough to ask for the abrogation of this regulation. I say this with great earnestness. This is my appeal to the shippers of western Canada.
I understand there are many reasons why this regulation has been made. The interests of the British ship owner have been considered. The British people rely to a large extent upon the invisible asset of the earnings of the British ship owners, and this fact should be given consideration in arriving at any arrangement of this character. I am told, although I do not know myself, that this regulation has, to a degree, been made in his interests. He is a factor and is entitled to consideration, and for this additional reason I suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that they do not raise this question. This matter was not arrived at by this government under the conference agreements, it is a position which has been established and is now maintained by the British government under its own legislation without respect to conditions pertaining in Canada or the consent of the Canadian government. I do not think there is the slightest evidence to substantiate the innuendos and insinuations of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) that there has been a secret understanding
between the two governments in regard to this matter. The position is absolutely plain and he who reads the printed word may read it. It was something which transpired previous to the month of August, 1932.

What is the world price? The world price heretofore has been determined by Liverpool. Now we propose, by this duty of two shillings per quarter, as far as we possibly can, to put _ every bushel of Canadian wheat into the British market to the exclusion of the otheT countries of the world. What is the greatest

United, Kingdom,
volume of wheat that has ever gone into the British Isles for their own consumption? Article 4 reads:
On first sale in the United Kingdom at prices not exceeding the world prices and in quantities sufficient to supply the requirements of the United Kingdom consumers.
What does that mean? What are the requirements cf the United Kingdom consumers? Does that mean just the 45,000,000 or so people in Great Britain? Are we compelled only to give them just as much as will feed them, or does this mean that importers in Britain can, if they so choose, take 400,000,000, 500,000,000 or
200.000.	000 bushels of wheat out of Canada? Have we to give them everything they want, because if those are the requirements, they may take that wheat and mill it, meeting our millers in competition in the export markets. These are some of the questions I should like the minister to answer.
The first question I asked was:	What was
meant by "first sale?" Where will the price be determined? Heretofore Liverpool has been the basis of world wheat prices. If you are going to confine the British market and Britain is not going to set the price for her own wheat, but says she will take the world price, we must be going to move from Liverpool to some other point in Europe the right to set the price of wheat that we, the Canadian producers, will receive from the British importer. I think that is the position in which we are. Great Britain has the right under this agreement, to take all her requirements from Canada. Even supposing she were to do so, all you are doing is merely displacing that portion of Argentine, Russian or Australian wheat that now finds a place in the British market. You are releasing that from the British market and putting it on to the European market. Supposing she took all of ours, then that inferior wheat-and I say so advisedly-coming from those countries, is going to be the standard to determine the value of our wheat sold in the British market. You are not giving to the producer in western Canada an iota of difference in the price that he w'ould get if this agreement did not exist. If the British people want to exercise their right under this agreement, they can take 200,000,000 or 3,00,000,000 bushels of wheat, as the case may be.
I have the figures here of the importations into the British Isles from all countries, and of wheat that has found a place on the export market. The United Kingdom in 1915 imported only 165,000,000 bushels; in 1916,

bushels. Between 1915 and 1931 the largest import which the United Kingdom made of wheat was 222,000,000 bushels last year, and that w'as from all sources. What was the production of Canada last year? It was away in excess of 222,000,000 bushels. In fact, we carried over from the previous year 130,000,000 bushels that we had no market for at all, and we have now probably in the neighbourhood of 500,000,000 bushels. Even if Great Britain took all her wheat requirements from Canada, the most she has taken in any year from 1915 to 1931 was 222,000,000 bushels, so that we would still have about 350,000,000 bushels that would have to compete with the wheat of Australia, Russia, the Argentine, and any other country with an exportable surplus, and that competition would decide the price not only of the 222,000,000 bushels but of the whole wheat crop of Canada. It simply means that you are doing just as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough said you were doing in regard to fish. We will get no more for our wheat, but if the producers of the Argentine, Russia, and other countries with an exportable surplus ship their wheat to Great Britain they will receive six cents less. The world supply will determine the price of Canada's wheat; it will determine what the farmer on the western plains of Canada will get for his crop.
I will go this far and say that the Prime Minister before that conference maintained one note, and it was that he would .do nothing and see that nothing was done that would jeopardize the efficient industries of Canada. What I want to ask the Prime Minister is this: Did they carry that doctrine into effect when they brought about this agreement respecting the disposition of our wheat? I think they did, and I think they were ill-advised. My hon. friend from York-Sunbury says that the Canadian government had nothing to do with this. But surely the Prime Minister and the other Canadian delegates considered the effect that this would have on the largest portion of Canada's wheat crop, because the whole of the crop is affected, not simply the portion that is going to the British Isles. Not only that, but if you will go through the statistics you will find that in many years 300,000,000 bushels of wheat left the shores of Canada destined for Great Britain but never reached that country because it was diverted while on the ocean. So far as the producers in Canada are concerned, make it possible for us to ship our wheat through all-Canadian channels and I think

speechtext:
I will deal first with
the question asked by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). He suggested that there was some secret arrangement with respect to this matter. There was no such arrangement. I should think he would have been satisfied on that point when I read to him the other day the reply to the message which had been sent to London in order that misapprehension, if any, might be relieved. If there had been an arrangement wre would not have been asking the British authorities as to the interpretation placed upon the article in the agreement.
I can only say this, that so far as the agreement as it stands at the moment is concerned, and it will not be altered 'because it has been adopted by the British parliament, it provides just what it says, namely, that goods in order to secure the preference must be the product of the empire, and they must be consigned to the United Kingdom. The regulation that I read the other day is a regulation, I find, which was in force before this agreement was adopted. It is the standard regulation which Great Britain has had in use in dealing with matters of this kind.
I did, after the discussion in the house the other day, communicate with Winnipeg for the purpose of ascertaining just what the exact words were in use by the grain business in dealing with shipments through Buffalo. I secured those words, and prepared a cable to ask the British authorities if the regulation covered those words. I have not a reply, for the cable has not yet been sent, as a matter of fact, because the grain dealers in Winnipeg intimated that one cf their number might come here. As a matter of fact, he did net come although I thought he was on the way. That is the position so far as the question asked by the hon. member for Lisgar is concerned.
There is no doubt that the question has been much discussed and much debated in all parts of this dominion, and there has been an increasingly strong opinion that if the west is to secure all the advantages which it hopes for from time to time-we have made very large advances to western provinces during the last few months; we have loaned them large sums of money and carried on enormous expenditures; in addition the question was asked the other day whether the government had bought

grain, to which question I deferred the answer until Monday, but I may say now that the government has not itself purchased grain but did assist one of the enterprises that is owned by the people of western Canada to do so for reasons that I shall indicate next Monday- there is an increasingly strong opinion that Canadian ports should be utilized by one of the greatest Canadian industries if in turn it is bo ask for and receive always every consideration from the government of the day. This government is not the only government which has shown itself sympathetic to Canadian industry in the form of agriculture, for it is the greatest of Canadian industries. In addition, the purchasing power icf the people is at once reflected by the sale of Canadian grain in the fall. The ability to purchase the products of eastern Canadian factories or of factories abroad is at once reflected by the volume of business that is transacted every year through the sale of grain. It is in a sense the easiest and most rapid way that we have bo create new wealth except, if the hon. member for Willow Bunch will pardon me, by the securing of petroleum from the earth, which has been said by one economist to be the shortest and quickest way to create new wealth because petroleum can be converted into products very salable by the expenditure for machinery of a very small sum of money, say
S30,000,	under the old-fashioned way of refining. Of course, there is always gold. That is new wealth without refining, but it is rarely found in large quantities except in the alluvial deposits of some rivers. But wdieat creates new wealth easily and quickly ficr the reason that under our present methods we have a complete system established of elevators and terminals whereby the farmer hauls his grain to the elevator and the elevator gives him a ticket, under the Grain Act. The elevator man may have a limited amount of capital, perhaps just enough to own a single elevator, but from the bank he secures an advance based upon the hypothecation of the grain he has 'bought. Then the bank insists that he shall hedge his purchase, which means that for that immediate cash sale there is an exchange for a future sale. From that it at once follows that the price of the grain immediately goes into circulation, not simply the 20 per cent which the borrower has been able to borrow from the bank, but the price of the whole of the grain. That is why there is such an extension of credits in the fall under the Finance Act; the whole price of the grain is at once set in circulation, the banks provide the necessary credits for the balance between the margin that the operator has as capital and the price paid-and he has the facilities,-and that is

United Kingdom
the reason that the east as well as the west has been so interested in the harvesting of a large crop, and in its rapid movement out of the country. That is the reason that this year, although the price is very low, the crop being large, there has been realized for circulation in western Canada a very large sum of money, I should think /between seventy-five and a hundred million dollars. That is a large sum of money to set free in any area, especially one with a population of less than two and a half million souls.
The movement out of this country is of course of primary importance to every one. Through the harbour of Montreal there moves out of this country not only a large part of the Canadian crop, but an enormous number of bushels of the American crop. The reason for that is fairly obvious; all one has to do is to look at the map to realize and understand it. I say to my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) I have not been in sympathy with the construction of storage facilities at Buffalo, I think they might have better been put on the Canadian side. The movement from the storage facilities has been dealt with by the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance); it is a matter about which opinions will always differ. But it is certain that many countries would have insisted by legislation that the movement should be through Canadian ports. One of the conditions under which the British preference is accorded is that the movement of the goods shall be through British ports. Two exceptions are made, I mentioned one the other day, the port of Beira in connection with the movement out of Southern Rhodesia. There are similar conditions with respect to other ports. For instance, sometimes shipping is not available, it became necessary in one instance to which my attention was directed last week that an order in council should be passed under the provisions in that behalf, authorizing it to provide for a movement that was not wholly through British or Canadian ports. As far as this section is concerned it was on the statute books of the United Kingdom in March, 1932. When the matter came up for discussion at the Ottawa conference it was one that was as important in a sense to Australia though not to the same extent, and to other countries that ship their goods to Great Britain, as it was to us. In the end the section remains as it is, and the construction placed upon it is: (a) the commodity must originate in the British Empire; (b) the commodity shall be consigned to the United Kingdom; and (c) that if it is either on a through bill of lading, as I mentioned the
other day, or identified by documents authenticated by the authorities that the British government have always chosen for that purpose, namely their consuls, which is the common practice I may say of all countries, vised by the consul, then the goods are treated as having been identified from the point of origin to the point of ultimate destination. That has been the condition imposed.
But because of the discussion that took place I have endeavoured to secure further information upon it, and the result of my inquiry was the telegram I read to the house the other day from the High Commissioner's office, which embodied the exact terms handed to them in writing by the Dominions' Office. Obviously in a matter of this kind I think the hon. gentleman from Lisgar would realize that no government would think of making any secret arrangement with respect to the construction to be placed upon a public document. It is solely within the power of the British authorities to determine the regulations under which the conditions imposed are met. But those conditions are statutory, and cannot be changed except by act of parliament of the United Kingdom. They involve: (a) origin within the empire; (b) consignment to the United Kingdom on a through transit-if I might use that word-although the transit might be interrupted; but as long as the point of origin is fixed, and the destination is the United Kingdom, even though there were delays in the transit, the preference applies.

With respect to the value of the preference, I am in no sense critical of discussion in the house of commons, but it has been discussed in the house at great length. Our view on this side is that it is part of the agreement which we propose to try, and we believe it is in the interests of the Canadian producer. Of course, first sale means, as I think the hon. gentleman realizes, the sale made to the importer of the wheat in question. As far
1046	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
as world's prices are concerned, that is a term applicable to the metal market, the sugar market, the tea market, the cotton market, the coffee market, all these are matters which in trade parlance are affected by what is called the world's market, the world's market price, for instance the Baltic, Mincing Lane, the Cotton Producers' exchange of New York and institutions of that kind. You will observe in this very agreement a provision that the Metal Exchange is to be the determining body with respect to prices in connection with some of these metals. For instance, the contracts that were made in connection with oil from the Turner valley, when I was actively interested in the business there, provided that the price current appearing in a given journal published in Oklahoma should be the governing price. That is a matter that businessmen agree to. In this instance the world's price is the price that is current in the world, it is predicated upon the assumption that the hon. gentleman who has just sat down has strongly urged, namely, that there is a much larger production of wheat in Canada than the United Kingdom could take. It therefore follows that the price will not be fixed by that demand alone, but by the law of supply and demand. And that fixes the price for the first sale. The price at which the commodity could be purchased by any one desiring to purchase it on the open market of the world for sale anywhere would be the world's price for the commodity. And if, as I said the other evening, the British miller prefers to purchase wheat outside the British Empire he may do so, but if he does he will pay two shillings more for every eight bushels than if he had bought Australian or Indian or Canadian wheat. If he buys Esthonian or French wheat he will pay two shillings a quarter more than if he had bought Canadian or Australian wheat.
The circumstances under which this agreement was arrived at as far as wheat is concerned will be found indicated to some extent in the observations made by Mr. Graham in 1923 at the economic conference. I need not dwell upon the fact that for at least a generation-I can only speak about one, I have lived in western Canada thirty-five years- for at least the lifetime of a generation there has been urged by the farmers of the west the value of a preference for wheat in the British market. This preference has now been secured. If as hon. gentlemen think, it does not work out as satisfactorily as we hope, then of course we shall be disappointed and sorry. If it works out as we believe it will 
the effect will be to afford a larger market for Canadian wheat, but not at a higher price. We did not expect to be able to demand a higher price for our commodities; no one has suggested that. A few days ago the right hon. leader of the opposition spoke of the poor in England paying a higher price for their food. That effect always has been apparent to everyone who has thought about this matter, and there is no provision in this agreement that contemplates the poor paying a price higher than the world price. But in order that there might be no opportunity for the assertion that an effort had been made to place an undue burden upon the people of England by way of an enhanced price for Canadian or Australian wheat you will see that the world price is to govern, because the surplus of this country for export exceeds any possible importations that could be made by Great Britain.
I do not think there is anything I can usefully add to what has been said so frequently from this side of the house. The criticisms of hon. gentlemen opposite are upon record. If we are wrong and they are right we suffer and they gain; our judgment will have been in error and their criticisms will have been well founded. But we do suggest that the conditions warrant any government securing, if possible, a sheltered market for wheat for Canada and other parts of the British Empire, in the greatest importing wheat market in the world.

No, not just now. This is my point: Now you are going to divert our wheat to the British market, perhaps to the extent of 222,000,000 bushels, but the European market will determine what price is to be paid for that wheat. Selling in that European market will be the surplus of our wheat which we cannot put on the British market, the Russian wheat, the Argentine wheat and the Australian wheat, which does not compare in quality with the wheat that is being sheltered, as the Prime Minister says, in the British market. On that wheat of inferior quality will be determined the price we will get for our 222,000,000 bushels exported to Great Britain, if that country chooses to take advantage of the agreement into which we are now entering.
That is the point. Not only that, but the wheat of all countries is not assembled as our wheat is, as the Prime Minister well knows. Argentine wheat sells on an f.a.q. basis, fair average quality. They jumble all their w'heat together and it is sold on the basis of the fair average quality. We do not do that; we grade our wheat, and sell it by grade. The point I am making is that the portion of our wheat sent to the mother country will be obtained for less than we would receive otherwise, because of the fact that she is not now determining the value of that wheat; it is being determined outside her boundaries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I will amplify what I said by only a few sentences. World wheat prices are not settled in Liverpool; the mathematical computations are carried on there and at the Baltic, which is an entirely different matter. World wheat prices are determined by supply and demand, and whenever the supply is so much in excess of the demands of the importing countries as it is today, when the entire demand for wheat for a whole year could be supplied by the surplus in exporting countries with practically no new crop being grown at all, the result is a completely demoralized market. W'herever there is no demand and a surplus supply, that supply is offered in the markets of the world at a price which very often bears no relation to the cost of production. The circumstances under which the wheat market of the world has
broken since 1929 could be related as chapters in a story that follow so simply that no argument would be required to convince this house that the whole factor that determines prices is supply and demand, plus one other factor, the willingness of any one producing country to take any price at all for its product in order to undersell its competitors. That condition did arise at one time with respect to one country. I told this committee once that in 1930 I asked a Canadian to go to Liverpool and look at a cargo of wheat that had arrived there the day before and that was being sold for 60 cents a bushel at the dock, which was less than Canada, Australia or the Argentine were asking for their wheat, having regard to quality. As most hon. gentlemen know, the wheat grown in the northern part of Russia is not vastly different from the very best of Canadian wheat. This wheat was offered at a price calculated to undersell any competitor who might sell his wheat on the basis of showing a profit in production. That is the basis of all sales. When wheat went to S3 in the markets of the world, as perhaps hon. gentlemen will recall, in Canada it went from a little over $2 in the fall to over $3 in the spring, and wheat stored in elevators by Canadian farmers returned a very large profit. Why was that? It was because the expectations with respect to production in certain parts of the world were not realized, and the supply fell far short of what it was expected to be while the demand was constant.
That is the position. So far as the present condition is concerned I can only repeat that the price is not fixed at Liverpool. The mathematical computations, in which the figures are assembled for the purpose of knowing what wheat is available to meet the demands, are largely carried on there. The one great authority in the world is Broomhall, and as everyone knows Broomhall's figures at the moment are to the effect that something like
705,000,000 bushels will be required this year to meet the requirements of importing countries. He points out also that the quantity available, taking in United States wheat, is practically double that figure. The whole question that had to be considered was the extent to which the production that was ripening in the southern hemisphere, namely in Australia and Argentine, would affect the market by reason of the market already being overloaded with a supply that far transcended the demand. I understand the effect has been a reduction in price because of the willingness of some countries to offer wheat for a price

Trade Agreements
lower than that obtaining before these crops came upon the world market in competition with existing surpluses.
I only desire to make it quite clear to the hon. gentleman that when we say Liverpool fixes a price we only say that the computations based upon Broomhall's very carefully considered estimates, both on the Baltic and at Liverpool, are computations that are based upon daily reports as to crop conditions. Violent winds have swept over areas in the southern hemisphere and the crop of yesterday has become a ruin, the effect being at once reflected in the market the next day. For instance, in western Canada we have all seen a magnificent crop of yesterday converted into no crop at all tomorrow, in very substantial areas, and that is reflected in the computations that are made by Broomhall's as to the available surplus to meet the market demands the succeeding day. When the world's supply and demand is mentioned as reflected in the world price, it is based on a well known and definite practice, and instead of endeavouring to define all the factors that constitute the world price, this agreement is made in that broad and generous * outline that would be expected on the part of Canadians making a bargain with their fellow citizens in Great Britain. We apprehend no difficulty, we have experienced none, nor have we any evidence of any with respect to this or any other clause.

speechtext:
For reasons that are well
known to the members of this house, I have not been able to follow1 very closely the discussion of the agreements made at the imperial conference. I did not expect, coming here this afternoon, that the question of the transportation of Canadian wheat through Canadian or American ports to the British Empire would be discussed. I thought that, under the sections of the agreement which I have read, it would not be quite in order to discuss that point of view, but since the discussion of it has been allowed, I wish to raise my voice as a representative of New Brunswick in behalf of our Canadian ports. As I understand it, our friends from the west have not, so far, raised any great objections to the shipment of wheat through Canadian ports. They have hinted, to some extent, their desire that the agreement might not, for the sake of the British preference, confine the shipment of Canadian wheat entirely to shipment through Canadian ports.
When we look at the record, I think it will be agreed that we, in the maritimes, are safe in claiming, as our western friends

claimed when money was expended for the accommodation of storing wheat at Buffalo, that what has been spent has been spent economically. We in the maritime provinces have worked along economical lines in the past and at the port of Saint John, for a certain period, without any help from any government in Canada, we have expended millions of dollars to prepare the harbour for the shipment of Canadian goods through that Canadian port. Later on, the government came to the assistance of the city of Saint John -I am not now referring to dredging and operations carried on in the past by other governments, but to recent expenditures. The government of the day came to the assistance of the city of Saint John, taking over the works on which they had expended in the neighbourhood of three or four million dollars, in order to prepare that harbour for export trade, to receive Canadian goods passing through a Canadian port. Since that time, without taking into account the money expended in consequence of the disastrous fire in the harbour of Saint John, the government has expended between ten and eleven million dollars to provide accommodation for shipping. It was not to provide accommodation for the shipping of foreign goods but to enhance the shipping value of a Canadian port, so that we in the province of New Brunswick as well as the people of Nova Scotia might do our share in the development of Canadian trade. When the government in 1923 or 1924 laid down the principle of an additional 10 per cent preference on goods coming through Canadian ports, we extended the facilities in the harbour of Saint John. Let me point out that all this was done for reasons of economy; not only was the province of New Brunswick interested along economical lines, but the whole dominion was so interested, because Saint John and Halifax were the only winter ports on the Atlantic coast, and in order to play our part we were prepared to make sacrifices. It is well known that we in the maritimes did all we could to assist the provinces of the west as well as central Canada.
Now, if the cheap rate of shipment is a question with our friends out west, let me point this out, that freight rates by rail and water combined are lower from the bay ports to Saint John and Halifax than they are to New York, by 3 or 4 cents per hundred pounds. If that is so, if from Port Colborne you can ship wheat down through the maritimes, landed at Halifax or Saint John, for 17-15 per hundred pounds, whereas from the same point of shipment to the central port of New York you have to pay 2 or 3 cents more, I want to

United Kingdom
know where the saving is to the western farmer. They tell me the saving would be on the water rates. If that is so, surely some arrangement can be made, in connection with our Canadian vessels using Canadian ports, to give a rate that would equalize the American.
As to the quantity of wheat which we may be able to handle, let me point out that in 192S-and we shall have greater facilities next spring or summer

we handled from 30 to 32 million bushels of wheat at that port, and the only reason we did not handle more was that it did not come. Of that 30 or 32 million bushels of wheat handled at Saint John that year, no less a quantity than 10 million bushels was American wheat. Our friends will say, yes, but if this agreement goes into effect the Americans will ship their wheat through their own port. Well, let them do so and it will give us more room to ship our Canadian wheat through Canadian ports. That is the stand I take in this matter.
If our western friends are afraid that we have not the facilities at Montreal, Vancouver, Saint John and Halifax to ship all Canadian grain that can be sold either in England or in other countries of the world, let me disabuse their minds of that idea. We can handle it. Montreal alone can handle hundreds of millions of bushels. The port of Saint John, if the wheat is sent in a proper way, in the winter season, from the month of December until May, can handle from 35 to 50 million bushels.

speechtext: No.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Someone says no. It may not be greater but it will be no less than that. I do not know as to the capacity at Halifax, therefore I shall not speak on that matter.
I should like to give a few figures in connection with freight rates. The freight rate from Midland, Ontario, to St. John, Halifax and Portland is 15.17 cents per hundred pounds, while the rate from Midland to New York is 22 cents. The rate from Port Col-borne, Ontario, to Halifax, St. John and Portland is again 15.17 cents, while the rate from Port Colborne to New York is 17.50 cents and will be 18.50 cents after November 23 when a change comes into effect.
I do not desire to say anything which might be detrimental to the interests of any party, especially my hon. friends in the west. I know they have been suffering not only from low prices but from crop failures but let me say to them that they are not the only ones in agriculture who have suffered. We in the maritime provinces have suffered just as great hardships in proportion to population. What
wheat is to the western farmer, potatoes are to the farmer in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. We too have had failures in crops. The largest crop produced today in New Brunswick is the potato crop. When the planting took place this year the prospects looked splendid, it was expected that we would have the largest crop ever produced but, the blight came along and we will not take out more than forty or fifty per cent of what we put in the ground. The farmers in the west have suffered from drought but we in New Brunswick have suffered from the blight. I do not know what conditions prevail in the other maritime provinces but I know that the conditions in New Brunswick are pitiful so far as the farmers are concerned. While we feel for our friends in the west, while we are prepared to cooperate in anything that is reasonable in order to help them, as I know and feel they cooperated with us a few years ago when the question of better terms for out provinces was up, let me say to them in all seriousness that we feel we are doing no injustice to the west when we stand up for what we consider to be the rights of the maritime provinces. As a representative from that section of Canada I appeal to other sections to join hands with us to help us along in obtaining what is our due in the matter of transportation.
It must be remembered that if it were not tor the maritime provinces there might have been no western Canada. When confederation was mooted in 1867 the maritime provinces came in under the distinct understanding and contract that certain things would be done. Ontario and Quebec asked the maritime provinces to join with them in order to provide an outlet to the Atlantic coast so that they would not have to depend upon American ports for the shipments of goods to the British Empire. We came into confederation on the strength of certain promises which have never been carried out to the full extent. We have suffered and made sacrifices in the past, we are prepared to make sacrifices in the future; we will do our share to bring about prosperity and progress in this fair Canada of ours but I hope we will not be called upon to make sacrifices which we consider to be too great. A sacrifice which I consider to be too great is to consent to. the diversion of Canadian trade from the maritime provinces to American ports.

speechtext:
The hon.
member for South Battleford has had his say and as I do not intend to take very long I ask him to let me continue.
It is contended that this pact will give Canada an assured market for a very considerable portion of her surplus. We hear hon. members opposite say that what we need is more and wider markets; those are vague terms which they seem to love but for the life of me I cannot understand why, when they get a practical market assured to them, they say it is of no value. This trade agreement assures to Canada a certain market for a considerable portion of her exportable wheat surplus each year. We say that that should be of some value.
Let us try to envisage what will happen each year. The British buyers of wheat will bid to the world sellers for their products and Canada will come to the forefront along with the United States, with the Argentine and other exporters of wheat. Let us see whether or not this pact puts us in a preferred position. A man close to a market has an advantage over a man distant from a market, as hon. members from the west well know. Why? Because if it costs a farmer

at a distant point six cents a bushel to market his wheat, he is to that extent at a disadvantage. If I have a farm close to a market where I can sell my wheat, and if I save six cents in mileage or freight rates, I am that much better off than the man distant from the market although we are both selling at the world1 price. Am I not in a preferred position over a man further removed when I can save six cents a bushel freight rate on my wheat? Then, let us apply that to the situation in question. It is a question, not of mileage, but of preference, and whether Canadian producers get a preference of six cents a bushel by reason of a shorter haul or by reason of some other preference, it is six cents a bushel just the same, although the world price is the same. Without extending the matter further, let me put it in this way, and I submit that this is true: When world sellers seek entry into the British market, the Canadian producer of wheat will get in that market the world price. Those who do not enjoy the preference given in this pact will get what if they want to enter the British market? They will receive the world price less six cents a bushel. Hon. members may say that we have not influenced the world price of wheat. That is no doubt true, but the Canadian producer of wheat will get the world price, and those who have not the benefit of this pact will get the world price less six cents a bushel. Is there no advantage in that?
Let me put the matter in just one other form and then I shall have finished: Hon. members opposite decry this agreement; they say that it is no good. The United Kingdom has given us a preference of six cents a bushel on our wheat. Let me put the matter conversely. Supposing Canada were not able to have that preference; supposing the United Kingdom negotiated a treaty, not with Canada but with the United States, and supposing under that treaty the United States was given a preference of six cents a bushel in the United Kingdom market and Canada was not. What then would hon. members from the west say? Supposing Canada were not in this pact but that Australia was, that the Argentine was; that Russia or some other country was, and that they were given the six-cent preference and we were not. 1 think I have only to put that possibility to the committee fior any man to envisage, to realize what an outcry would come from producers of grain in the Dominion of Canada. I hesitate to suggest the headlines that would appear in all the western press irrespective of party politics. I hesitate ho think what the hon. member for South Battleford, if faced

United Kingdom
with such a situation, would say in this house. Then, indeed, you might hear, and perhaps with some reason, in various centres in this country, of the beginning of a movement to secede from the empire. What would this be called? It would be called discrimination against Canada, for which Canada would not stand, and I doubt whether Canada would stand for it. So I say that we can measure the benefit to Canada by virtue lof this preference in terms of the disadvantage she would suffer if a like preference were given to the United States and not to this dominion.

speechtext:
After the speech from
the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot), I feel that there is very little more which need be said from the point of view of the maritime provinces with regard to this matter of the routing of Canadian grain. I am sure we all share in the pleasure of seing the hon. member for Gloucester back again in the house. It is a great pleasure, particularly to us from the maritimes, to hear him in his characteristic style, standing up for the part -of the country from which he comes. It would be almost painting the lily for me to add anything to what he has said.
I just want to remind our western friends of this: If we from the maritime provinces had been writing the agreement, we might well have requested the government at least to endeavour to insist on the word "port" being inserted in article 1 instead of "part," so that it would ensure that grain to receive the benefit of the preference would have to go through Canadian ports. Those are the terms under which the 10 per cent additional preference is permitted under our Canadian tariff. That has not been done. The word "part" is used in the agreement, permitting the British government to make regulations whereby goods coming from a part of the British Empire, even though they are actually shipped from some foreign port, may be given the preference. I say to my hon. friends that we from the maritimes might complain of that. On the other hand, they complain that the agreement has not gone further so as to permit the preference to be extended, not only to goods which are in direct transit, but also to goods which may have been stored at a United States port. This seems to have been a compromise, and one which the Prime Minister quite frankly says was not stipulated for by the Canadian government but was part of the British regulations under the Import Duties Act.

My right hon. friend corrects me-and I accept his correction-that it was in force even before the Import Duties Act was passed, or in other words, is a part of the British administration of their act with regard to duties. But when I "Say that, I say at the same time, and I hope my hon. friends from the west will not consider it as any empty expression, that I do not forget, and the people of the maritimes will not forget, the support which was given by our friends from the west about three years ago in connection with the matter of freight rates in relation to the question of maritime claims. All we ask them now is, that if this agreement is to pass, they join in giving this method of administration a chance and not press further than the agreement and the regulations already provide, for the elimination of Canadian ports. Canadian ports, under the agreement as it stands, can now be sidestepped to some extent. Great ports have been established on both the maritime and the western seaboards where large expenditures have been made. Those ports have been regarded as national assets and national expenditures have been made in the interests of the people, not only of the maritimes but of Canada generally. Let me conclude by saying I join sincerely and heartily in the views which have been so admirably expressed by the hon. member for Gloucester.
Mr. ROWMAiN: I wish to say a word or two with respect to the remarks of the hon. member for YorknSunbury (Mr. Hanson) who introduced this discussion, following the question of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). Let me just remind hon. members from the maritimes on both sides of the house that after all the sale of wheat is purely a business proposition, and that the difference of a fraction of a cent, a quarter or an eighth of a cent in the quoted price may mean the sale or loss of sale of millions of bushels. Consequently it is extremely important that the lowest possible cost of transportation should rule in the shipment of grain. Our freight rate structure in the west is built up very largely on the competition which our sale of wheat has met with in the open markets of the world.
Shortly after the hon. member for Cumberland made his remarks in the house the other day, I spoke to him with regard to this question. I was in some doubt what rates were in force from the eastern lake ports to Halifax and Saint John, and I was told by him that very recently the Board of Railway Commissioners had put into effect a special rate for the month of November which was equal to about six cents a bushel. Hon. members from the maritimes should bear in mind that this is the first time that wc have had this special rate, and that up to the present there has been very little to induce the western grain dealer to ship his grain to Halifax and Saint John if the overland route was to be followed. Undoubtedly the overland route could not have been used by grain dealers for the shipment of grain with the old rates prevailing. It must be clear also to hon. members when appeals are made to the wrest that it is not the western farmer who has anything to do with the routing of his grain. He sells his grain to the dealer, and the dealer in the ordinary course of business seeks the cheapest route so far as carrying charges are concerned, no matter whether it be via Montreal, Buffalo or some other port. It is purely a business proposition. Consequently if the maritimes are to appeal to the west on this proposition they must be able to show to the grain dealer of the west that the5r have a route available over which grain can be shipped as cheaply as over any other route. So far from there being any feeling in the west as against the use of maritime ports, I can assure hon. gentlemen from the maritimes that there is none, and more than that, the west would be more than pleased

if we could utilize our owm eastern ports and, in addition, our own Canadian railway transportation system in shipping that grain to the eastern ports.

Before taking my seat may I refer to the remarks of the hon. member for South Battle-ford? Frankly I cannot follow him when he contends that our wheat will be offered at a lower price upon European markets.

That leaves just that much less quantity to be sold in the European markets in competition with the grain of other grain-producing countries of the world. Consequently, to say the least, it will not have any effect upon reducing prices. Personally, so far as I am concerned, it does seem to me that this preference is going to give just what the government intended that it should give, namely, an assured and stable market in the United Kingdom for a substantial portion of our grain at the world's price.

I think
the Prime Minister's statement has cleared up any difficulty I had over some of those newspaper reports. Regulation 12 in itself is plain enough. It will be found at page 576 of Hansard:
When empire goods consigned to Great Britain or Northern Ireland have been transshipped en route, or have been shipped from a foreign port after overland transit from the enipire country of origin, the importer at the time of making entry will be required to produce the through bill of lading or railway consignment note from the country of production to Great Britain or Northern Ireland in support of the certificate of origin.
I think that is plain enough. That is through transit. It goes on:
Where a through bill of lading or consignment note is not available, the invoice, local bill of lading or consignment note from the original point of origin, and a certificate of arrival or landing at, and exportation from, the port of transshipment will be required.
I think that also is perfectly plain. In the one case we have the one consignment note right through, and in the other the original note with the papers in connection with the shipment through. The Prime Minister stated today that the mere interruption of the through shipment alone would not interfere with the preference. The statement made by Mr. L. Hore-Belisha in the British house was somewhat disturbing. The amendment moved by Sir J. Sandeman Allen asked that grain consigned from an American port and certified by Oanadian government officer^ to have been grown in Canada should be entitled to t'he preference. The regulation calls for the original consignment note from the British country, but certified in connection with its transshipment through the foreign country. Quite different.
Since that debate in the British house, however, Mr. Chamberlain made a statement that appears in the Ottawa Citizen of November 4. Dealing with this matter, it says:
He then reiterated the government's stand that in order to gain the benefit of preference in the United Kingdom an article must not only have been grown or produced within the empire but must also have been consigned from an empire country.
"This does not mean," he elaborated, "that passage through another country necessarily deprives it of the preference. What it means is that in order to secure the preference it must be sent on a through note, and it is therefore open to the exporter in an empire country so to make his arrangements that when he makes his consignment he can accompany it by a through note and thereby secure the preference.
The whole question was whether it must be consigned through, either by the original consignment note and certificate, or whether interruption by storage would make it impossible to consign it through. I understand from the statement this afternoon that the interruption for a time does not do away with the possibility of consigning through and identifying the grain by the original consignment note, as stated in the regulation, with a certificate vised by the customs officer and by the British consul.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
would point out that we have two altogether different interpretations of this problem. According to the hon. member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Hanson) it appears that we cannot escape being penalized with an import duty of six cents if we ship wheat to England via Buffalo. On the other hand the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) thinks it will go through and escape being penalized as foreign wheat. That has got to be cleared up. But whichever way it goes it looks to me as if someone is going to get stung. If this wheat is to be forced to go out via Canadian Atlantic ports against heavy freight rates- though I understand they are not so heavy now-at a greater cost than via Buffalo, someone will have to pay the shot. I do not think there is any member on either side of this house who would not be delighted to see all our grain go by Canadian ports; I have always been in favour of that, but always with one condition, that it must not cost too much more than by the other route. About three-fifths, on the average, of our wheat that goes by the east Atlantic goes via Buffalo and if it goes that way as the hon. member for York-Sunbury seems to think if part of it enters Britain via that route it will be treated as foreign wheat and that they will levy the six cents duty on it entering Great Britain.
Surely it is not the purpose of the minister in this matter to set the west against the maritimes, because if that is his object he is not going to succeed; we are not going to have any altercation with the maritime provinces on this question. They are perfectly right in doing the best they can for their ports, but I suggest to them that the government must assume the responsibility for this. They were a signatory to this agreement, and if it was not properly dealt with or properly understood the government will have to accept responsibility. Let the maritime provinces appeal to the government and get a freight rate that will be as cheap as the way via Buffalo and all hands will be up for the Canadian maritime ports.

speechtext:
They have got that
rate now.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Well, they may
have; I understand they got it quite recently. Then our wheat should begin to roll down there. Some always does; in the winter time there is a certain amount of railway equipment required in the east to bring back supplies for the west, and that is one reason why a certain amount of overland haulage of wheat always took place, even in the old days, when there was no special rate. But what I want to point out is that there is a regulation in Great Britain preventing them from doing what they now want to do or what we possibly woidd like them to do. The British government can have this regulation changed tomorrow if they want to; it is not like the laws of the Medes and Persians which alter not. It is not like a part of this agreement, which cannot be changed, and I agree that it cannot without consulting the other contracting countries. But a regulation or even a law, can be changed in the British house. And since this government secured the abrogation of the Anglo-Russian treaty because they so badly wanted that done, surely they could have had this regulation changed if they wanted to. If they had pointed out that the interpretation now put on it by some would make it necessary to change the routing of the great part of the three-fifths of our transatlantic shipments from the route that has been in use for the last fifty years it might have appeared to all as unwise and unjust, especially without warning. The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) gave, the other day, the quantities moving by that route, and I will not repeat them. Our government must accept the responsibility for this, they were a party to these agreements-very much a party, I thought. It is up to them to see that our freight rates, not only on the lakes and by rail, but on the ocean also, shall not be higher by the eastern Canadian ports-if our wheat is to be forced that way-than by Buffalo and the American ports. Figures were given by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) and I think the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) showing that ocean rates from New York to Liverpool and other British ports are invariably lower than from Halifax to the same point. So it is up to the government by some means, subsidy or otherwise, to make the cost of carriage by our own ports as cheap as by the way the traffic has been going. Then the problem will be solved, and I am sure I would like to

see it solved in that way. But there is one way that I am not going to see it solved, and that is by quarrelling with the maritimes. It is up to them to see that the government meet their requirements, and it is up to us to see that they meet our requirements. If the government finds itself on the horns of a dilemma as between being stung by losing the six cent British import duty if shipment is made by Buffalo or paying four or five cents more by the Canadian ports, then it will have to choose which horn seems easier to ride on. I would like to see both horns taken off; let us dehorn the dilemma. The conference w'as held in this building, and this is the place where this real problem should have been threshed out.
On the 31st of October I asked this question of the Prime Minister:
Did the dominion government prepare for and submit to the Ottawa economic conference or any committee thereof, data and information bearing on the important problem of whether or not Canadian wheat when stored at Buffalo or other American ports and rebilled for export to the United Kingdom would be eligible to enter that market under the British preference of approximately six cents per bushel on Canadian and other dominion wheat.
The answer given by the Prime Minister
was:
I need hardly point out that the question relates to an imperial statute. Representations were made to the conference with respect to the matter. The British, being large shipowners, claimed the right, which they have exercised, to determine the conditions under which the preference provided by the statute would be granted. I can add nothing further to that.
My right hon. friend was much more submissive in that case than he was with respect to the Russian treaty. If my right hon. friend had seen the difficulty as we see it now he surely would have had some explicit understanding as to whether our wheat going via Buffalo would be looked upon as foreign wheat or Canadian wheat after being stored there say one to ten months. The Prime Minister must accept the responsibility that rests upon him and the other Canadian delegates, present, and we look to him to solve this question, either by interceding with the British government or by negotiating with the maritime provinces. If it is the deliberate policy of the British government to make the condition what some understand it to be, that wheat is eligible for consideration as preference wheat only if it goes through our ports, I have no doubt Great Britain will be ready to negotiate. This is one of the differences provided for in the agreement that may be

United Kingdom
adjusted. They may ask some quid pro quo if any change is made, but surely this is one of the problems that should be solved, not so much by scrapping over it as by earnest negotiations and personal interviews.
I think it is time the Minister of Trade and Commerce took a hand. He will not get very many hon. members to follow the militant lead of the hon. member for York-Sunbury. I think he was looking for a little scrap with someone, but we are not going to scrap on this question. The hon. member for Peace River seems to take quite an opposite view; he thinks it is all right, and I should like to know if the hon. member for Peace River has had any information from the minister, or if the minister has any information to give the rest of the house that may help solve this problem. Perhaps we are all talking to no purpose; perhaps the wheat will go through Buffalo and be stored there for any period up to ten months, and still receive the exemption from British import duty of six cents. I think ten months is the time limit, after which it is charged the regular duty of forty-two cents by the United States. The minister might throw a little light on that question, as to whether our wheat going through the United States will be recognized as Canadian wheat. I am disposed to think some means will be devised whereby that will be done. I wonder if the minister could not enlighten us, and perhaps shorten this discussion.
