speechtext:
Coming from a wheat growing district, and being a wheat grower myself, I must say that this question of the marketing of wheat is of prime importance to the people of western Canada. Two things must be taken into consideration in the marketing of wheat, first the price we are to get for that wheat and secondly the quantity w'e may sell. I know how interested the people in western Canada were when they heard talk of a six cent preference on wheat, and the possibility of getting that much more per bushel. I know what it meant to them, because I know that the condition of the wheat grower in western Canada today is almost hopeless.
I am sorry that I must agree with the Prime Minister when he says that this preference will mean nothing to the farmers of the west in the way of higher prices. The Prime Minister has said, and I have to agree with him, that this six cent preference will not give us a higher price for our wheat. I believe that all westerners understand that today. The second question, however, is with
regard to the quantity we may sell. The people of the west are very much alarmed over this trade pact, which they think will be a detriment to them; they are afraid it will interfere with their ordinary trade routes and hinder them from selling their wheat in the markets of the world. As we have been told, over sixty per cent of our wheat has gone through United States ports, and if that sixty per cent cannot enter the United Kingdom market under the terms of this agreement it must find a market in Europe, outside the British Empire.
My hon. friend from York-Sunbury referred to the possibility of shipping our wheat through the maritimes. I may say candidly that western farmers do not know how their wheat is sold. They would just as soon see it go through the maritimes as any other place; in fact we would rather see it go from Canadian ports if that could be done without any extra cost to the western farmer. At present, however, we must realize that there are only two or three exporting companies in Canada handling wheat. Years ago we had the pool, the western grain growers and a lot of other companies, but today three companies do practically all'the exporting of wheat, and those companies have their headquarters in Prance. They have agents here who buy the wheat and send it to the markets of the world. I do not know whether or not these people, in selling that wheat, can get around the matter of storage at Buffalo.
I believe the Prime Minister said that this matter was brought up and discussed at the conference. If it was discussed there and provision was not made for our exporters to ship through United States ports, then I say the government neglected their duty. It was their duty to see that our grain could be shipped through United States as well as Canadian ports. Someone has referred to the elevators built by the pool, the western grain growers and other companies at Buffalo and other places. Surely that does not concern us; it was up to those people to build their elevators wherever they thought best. These companies built their own elevators with their own money; if they built them in the wrong places it is just too bad for them.
There is no doubt that Buffalo holds a strategic position in regard to the export of wheat and there is no doubt that if our exporters could send our wheat through Saint John and Halifax and get it to the markets of the world as easily and as cheaply as it can be sent through New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and other places, our wheat would

go from Canadian ports. More than that, I believe that if western grain growers had any say in the matter, and if it could be done just as cheaply, they would send their wheat by the Canadian route, but the western grain growers have nothing whatever to do with the way the grain is sold. The people exporting grain take two things into account, first the cost of export and secondly the facilities available. We know that one of our chief means of shipment is by ocean liners from New York, where they have a floating elevator which fills the liners with wheat as ballast, which is carried at a very low rate. These liners will not come to Halifax and Saint John in order *to get that ballast; in fact they will not pull up to the elevator; the elevator has to come to them. That is why so much wheat goes through New York; it obtains that cheap freight rate.
Let me repeat that if our government, in drawing up this tardy pact, neglected to take into consideration this important point, theirs is the responsibility and they will have to take the blame or the praise as the case may be for having arranged it in this way. The hon. member for Peace River thinks we can ship our grain through United States ports and hold it in storage there, and still get the preference. I have discussed this question *with some men who ship grain, and they have told me they think it might be arranged. It might be done iby some sort of subterfuge. They say it might be shipped down the lake, consigned to England; the exporting companies will consign it all to the British Isles and they will have it held over in Buffalo or New York or somewhere there, and then ship when it suits them, on to England. Whether that is so, I do not know. I should like to have an explanation from the Minister of Trade and C-ommerce with regard to this. Will he tell us whether it is possible for that to be done or not? I repeat, so far as the maritimes are concerned, if we can ship through maritime ports as easily and as cheaply as through New York or Buffalo, then the western grain growers are ready to ship that way; but the Minister of Trade and Commerce should give us a clearcut opinion as to what we can do with regard to these shipments going through Buffalo at the present time.

It is not my wish to prolong the debate on this question. I might say, however, in the five or six minutes I will speak, that with us in the maritimes this has been a burning question for a great many years. I am very much pleased indeed to hear the expressions of goodwill from western mem-

bers on both sides of the house with reference to the maritime provinces and maritime province ports. The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) and the hon. member for WTllow Bunch, who have just spoken, are somewhat vague in their remarks, however. 0<j the one hand they hold out the olive branch to the maritime provinces, and especially the maritime ports of Saint John and Halifax, and apparently thejr try to convey to us in no uncertain tones the vast amount of goodwill and sympathy they have for us and our ports. Then they spoil their whole argument by turning round and trying to get the Minister of Trade and Commerce to assure them that there may still be some way out whereby their grain can flow through American ports. That is the phase of the argument that seems to spoil the whole thing.
In the maritime provinces the whole question of confederation still comes up frequently in political debate. It is a fact well known to any man who has studied the history of confederation that we in the maritimes were promised certain things by the rest of the dominion for the advantages which in our opinion we were losing in entering confederation. Our natural flow of trade before confederation was through the Atlantic seaboard. That is a story I will not go into now, but we were promised, upon entering confederation, that we should be linked up with the rest of the dominion by a railway system, and the Intercolonial railway was built accordingly. If anyone cares to look over the report of the Duncan commission, he will find that that commission went very thoroughly into these matters in 1926, and the commission states that the Intercolonial railway was built for the express purpose of inducing us to enter confederation-that it was purely a political road and was never intended to pay dividends on the money invested in it.
We have invested vast sums of money in terminals, elevators and docks in the seaports of Saint John and Halifax, and to us it is a great conundrum indeed why, after we have spent these huge sums of money in our railway system, in our docks and elevators at maritime province ports, they are not being used. We cannot understand it. We know that the bulk of the grain of the west will continue, during the open season of navigation, to flow down the St. Lawrence through the port of Montreal. We are satisfied with that; it is a Canadian route, a Canadian port. But when the St. Lawrence is frozen up we see no reason why a certain amount, enough to keep the elevators and railways busy,

United Kingdom
should not go through the ports of Halifax and Samt John rather than through American ports.
It has been said today that arrangements have been made with reference to freight rates, whereby if the western grain is shipped over this route the shippers will not suffer by reason of freight rates. Let me say that it is pretty nearly time that this arrangement was made. We own the railway and should be able to make such rates as would render it possible for this grain to flow over our own railway and through our own ports. Consider the situation as it is today. How many of our own Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario railway-men are walking the streets idle, some in the bread line, for want of work? And just think of the work it would give our own railways and railway employees if, during the winter season, a great share of this wheat could be diverted through Canadian ports. Think of the work it would give our own railway employees and the joy and happiness it would bring to their homes.
We in the maritimes have always loyally supported both central and western Canada in any of the great undertakings in which the dominion as a whole has been engaged. We made no kick in the maritime provinces when western Canada asked for the Hudson Bay railway. We contributed our fair share to the building of that railway, and we hope that when the port of Churchill is further developed it will result in great benefit to a certain section of western Canada which will us.e that port. We have contributed our fair share to the building of the rest of our railways. We have contributed our fair share to the building of the great canal system in central and western Canada-all this for the benefit of western Canada, especially with respect to wheat. We in turn now ask that the ports of Halifax and Saint John receive that measure of assistance which has been long denied them.

As a representative from the constituency of Halifax, I feel that this subject should not be dropped without a small contribution from me. I want to endorse what has been said by the representative from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) in bringing this matter to the attention of the house this afternoon. That hon. gentleman presented the case for the maritime ports very clearly and definitely. It is hardly necessary for me or any other representative from the maritimes to elaborate what he has said, except to endorse his representation and perhaps to add a word here and there to fill in some of the small gaps. For instance, some of our western friends, the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and others whom I have heard outside as well as in the house, seem to have some misgivings as to the facilities for handling grain shipped through Canadian Atlantic ports. I might be allowed to refer to a statement which should remove any doubts on that score. According to the export freight department of the Canadian National Railways, which I think should be sufficient authority, the cost of shipping bulk wheat from the so-called bay ports of the great lakes to Halifax and St. John by rail is less than the rail rate to New York and the same as the rail rate to Portland, Maine. The freight rate to St. John, Halifax and Portland from Midland, Ontario, is 15-17 cents per hundred pounds while from Midland to New York it is 22 cents. The rate from Port Colborne to Halifax, St. John and Portland is again 15-17 cents, but to New York it is 17-50 cents and will be 18-50 cents after November 23. I might point out that there is a special rate in effect at the present time for the fall movement of grain to the Atlantic ports. This is a rate of ten cents per hundred pounds and it meets the competition of the movement from Buffalo to New York where a similar rate prevails. I think these facts should remove any doubts or misgivings as to rates which our western friends have with regard to the shipment of Canadian grain through the ports of St. John and Halifax.
I have heard this afternoon of the considerable shipment of American grain through Canadian ports. The latest figures in this connection are for the calendar year 1931, and they show that the American grain shipped through Canadian ports during that period amounted to 12,050,000 bushels, while Canadian grain through United States ports amounted to 62,000,000 bushels. The United States grain passing through Montreal amounts to about one-fifth of Canadian grain passing through the port of New York.
I think I can remove any doubt there might be as to handling capacity. In Halifax the handling capacity is 30,000,000 bushels, while at Saint John it amounts to 65,000,000 bushels. This total of 95,000,000 bushels should take care of all the shipments to these two ports during the winter months.
Doubts have been expressed with regard to ocean tonnage. I have under my hand the latest schedule of steamship services from Halifax. This is issued by the harbour commission and shows that there are 181 fixtures

I say to him that he need have no fears on that score because the rates from all the ports on the Atlantic are competitive. They are about the same between Halifax and Liverpool as they are between New York and Liverpool. I am pleased to note the sympathy expressed by hon. members, particularly from western Canada. I am sure that this will be very pleasing to the people of the maritime provinces and I hope that it will mean the accomplishment of the efforts of the representatives from eastern Canada over a period of years. The result will be that the winter business, particularly of the ports of St. John and Halifax, will be benefited to such an extent as to warrant what has been said in their favour.

Mr. Chairman, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated a short time ago that no industry in the country produced so much new wealth in such a short time as did the growing of wheat. I agree with him in that statement, but I think he must agree that that new wealth is produced under such conditions that the farmer, the primary producer who produces the wealth, has none of it left for himself. One of the conditions which handicaps the western farmer is distance from his market. This fall the freight rate on wheat from Regina to Liverpool has been approximately thirty cents a bushel; every cent added to that freight rate is one cent subtracted from the price the farmer receives, every cent subtracted from that freight rate is one cent added to the price the farmer receives. That is a point which should be kept always in mind when considering this question.
My right hon. friend stated that there was no secret arrangement between his government and the British government in connection with the routing of our wheat through Canadian ports. We accept that statement; in fact, we never for a moment thought there was such an arrangement. However, when the agreement was being entered into between the

governments of Canada and Great Britain as to the preference on wheat it was the duty of our government to see that that agreement was worded in such a way that no British official could put an interpretation upon it which would prove injurious to our farmers. There is no doubt in my mind that the regulation of the British government, read last evening by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) and to be found on page 1034 of Hansard, will have the effect of diverting a certain amount of our wheat from American to Canadian ports. We are told that that will not affect the freight rate, and, therefore, will not affect the price. I ask this question: if our wheat can be sent through Canadian ports just as cheaply as it can be sent through American ports, why has it not gone through these ports before? Wheat will follow the line of least resistance, it will take the route where the freight is cheapest and the service is best. We are told that from now on the rates from Halifax and Saint John will be competitive with those from New York, and we accept that statement. If the New York rates advance, the maritime rates will advance; if the New York rates decline, our rates will decline.

They will be competitive. Let us see what effect this agreement will have upon rates. The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) has pointed out that the New York rates are controlled by the ocean liners sailing from that port to European ports. These vessels are always seeking a cheap cargo to serve as ballast and they are willing to carry wheat at a low rate. Such a practice would reduce the rates from New York, and, therefore, from the maritimes. This arrangement will eliminate this competition from the market. An ocean liner that is coming into New York and that has been in the habit of carrying wheat from there to Liverpool at six cents a bushel will find itself confronted with this condition, that before it can land that wheat at Liverpool it has to pay a six cent duty. Will they carry wheat at six cents a bushel any more? They will do one of two things: either demand a higher freight rate on that wheat or drop out of the market for wheat. If they demand a higher freight rate, the rate from New York increases and the competitive rate from the maritimes increases. If they drop out of the market, you have removed from it the controlling factor that has kept freight rates down. In either case

United Kingdom
freight rates from New York and also from the maritimes will advance. As I said before, every cent you add to the ocean or any other freight rate is one cent subtracted from the price which the farmer receives for his wheat. I say to my friends from the maritimes: We cannot afford that. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre is, I see, enthusiastic for this arrangement.

I am absolutely in
favour of any arrangement or agreement between any sections of the empire which will allow an all-Canadian routing of our commodities. There is a theory or philosophy of evolution, but so far they have been unable to find what they call the missing link. There is in the Canadian National railway system a forgotten link, which is the Transcontinental from Quebec to Winnipeg. For the last six successive sessions I have spoken in this house of the urgency and necessity of giving that transcontinental section a fair share of through traffic, so far as passenger, freight, grain and cattle traffic is concerned, from Winnipeg to the Atlantic seaboard; but so far, although I have received support from some members in the maritime provinces, I have not been successful.
I noticed this afternoon only one member mentioned the Transcontinental. I believe by this route we could very easily give to the western wheat growers and grain growers in general just as good rates as they are receiving at the present time on shipments through United States seaports. A few moments ago the hon. member for Weyburn said that freight follows the line of least resistance. That does not apply to Cochrane which is a divisional point between Winnipeg
53719-67^
and Quebec. If I buy a carload of flour for my trade, it has to go twice the distance necessary. It is billed not directly from Winnipeg to Cochrane, but by Fort William, North Bay and Cochrane, so that freight does not always follow the line of least resistance. I believe the Canadian people have not been treated fairly so far as the Canadian National Railway system is concerned in regard to giving the Transcontinental that through traffic for which it was originally built. The Duff report says that it cost an enormous sum of money to construct in the northern section in Canada one of the finest roadbeds there is on the North American continent, but with the exception of possibly two or three years when an experiment was carried on in the winter months, practically no grain from Winnipeg has gone through to the seacoast by this route. During the years that experiments were being carried on in connection with through traffic over that section, I received information that it cost the railway company, including a profit, eleven cents a bushel from Winnipeg to Quebec. When you consider that on that roadbed, on account of the extremely low grades and the very slight curvatures, you could haul a solid train of seventy-five full box cars, you will realize how the country has been cheated. If I understand the situation properly, any grain which is billed from the head of the lakes at Fort William to Buffalo will cost six cents a bushel. I do not know the exact rate from Winnipeg to Fort William, but it will be between four and six cents a bushel, so that a total of from ten to eleven cents will be paid to get the grain to a United States seaport. As I say, the experiments made prior to 1926 and during the winter months demonstrated that grain could be shipped from Winnipeg to Quebec via the Transcontinental for eleven cents a bushel. Under the present situation, as the railway employees are willing now to accept a reduction in their wages and also a decrease in mileage, I believe you could have the same haulage for at least from eight to nine cents a bushel, so on that score alone the country has been cheated to a large extent.
Although I belong, geographically speaking, to central Canada, I have always been sympathetic to the problems and claims of the maritime provinces, the three western provinces and British Columbia. I have always supported them loyally and listened to their arguments. Now I appeal to the western members that we in our section of the country have a grievance. If today we have a serious railway situation, it is partly due

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
to the fact that the National Transcontinental has not received its fair share of through traffic. In 1908, as a young man, I saw a cartoon in the Montreal Star explaining the wonderful qualities of the new Transcontinental railway running between Quebec and British Columbia, whereby it was believed the time to the Pacific coast would be reduced by from forty-eight to sixty-four hours. To make the situation plainer, there was a cartoon showing two polar bears running around the North Pole and saying the}' had the record time for through traffic in the northern section of this globe. I hat particular method of shipping has never been applied t.o our section of the country. Further than that, at the present time the rails are rusting from Quebec to Winnipeg; there is no through traffic from one city to the other. We have only a tri-weekly passenger service from Quebec to Cochrane and no service directly from Cochrane to Winnipeg and Vancouver. That is the situation as it affects every citizen of that section of the country. This question is of importance not only to my section but to Canada as a whole, because we maintain that this transcontinental, which cost over $100,000,000 to construct in order to give more direct communication from ocean to ocean, is not receiving its fair share of through traffic. The experiment that was made applied not only to grain but to cattle and heavy freight, which all proved to be profitable. Therefore, on this score, I must repeat to the hon. member for Wey-burn that there are certain occasions when even the natural law of freight following the line of least resistance has never been applied to our section of the country.
During the debate this afternoon it was asserted several times that sometimes the routing of grain or other commodities or even freight from England going to Canada was decided upon in, as one man said, France. I was told on several occasions by railroad men that the routing of freight in many cases was decided in Liverpool. The same man told me that with regard to some freight cargoes leaving Liverpool and supposed to unload in the city of Quebec, that freight, on account of the fact that the bill of lading gave directions to unload in Montreal, had to go to Montreal first and then come back to Quebec. This shows the hon. member for Weyburn that sometimes freight does not follow the line of least resistance. As I am correct in my appeal, I shall be glad to receive support from hon. members from the western provinces. I believe that no one of them is set

in his idea that no grain should be shipped through our section. I shall go further. When the winter season comes to the head of the lakes, the ports of Port Arthur and Fort William are closed earlier than is Montreal, and no grain is shipped from that section to the United States seaboard. If they apply the principle, to serve the purpose of which the original construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific was intended, wheat could go forward all through the year, even during the winter months, because, as I have said, experience during the months of December, January, February and April, show that the scheme is quite practical. I am glad the opportunity has been afforded to give the viewpoint not only of the maritime provinces, but also of central Canada, because we who happen to be in the latter section are not receiving our proper share of through traffic.
Although this has nothing to do with the present discussion, I regret that the Duff commission did not find it possible to visit our section of the railway, a section which cost the people of Canada $100,000,000, and which was primarily meant for through traffic and not local traffic, although the latter has developed in a way that even the promoters did not deem to be possible. Had the Duff commission visited that section they would have found out for themselves that there we have the finest roadbed, the finest curvatures and the lowest grades of any road in Canada or the United States, but you might as well take the rails away for all the attention the road is receiving, I will not say from parliament, but from the Canadian people as a whole, who do not seem to realize to the full the opportunities we have there of giving service not only to the eastern provinces but also to the three western wheat growing provinces of our confederation.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to hon. members advancing many reason why Canadian grain should be shipped by Canadian ports. I do not think I need tell this house that I am very much in sympathy with that argument. I also listened with great interest to the hon. members for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), Lisgar (Mr. Brown), and Weyburn (Mr. Young), who were in great gusto crying to the skies for permission to ship their wheat by

United. Kingdom
American ports, arguing why they should be permitted to ship by American ports in preference to Canadian. I find myself at a loss to understand why these gentlemen are advocating the shipping of wheat by American ports and why they are not concerning themselves with developing their own port at Churchill. The hon. member for Weybum made the statement that it cost thirty cents a bushel to ship wheat via Saint John and Halifax. May I point out that the rate per bushel on wheat from Regina to Churchill is 14-7 cents. In addition, the route is much speedier and certainly much safer than the St. Lawrence. That, I think, was amply demonstrated this year, when the Pennyworth landed flour in London just twenty days from the day the wheat was cut in Saskatchewan.
What is the history of this port of Churchill?
I have spoken of it several times. It was officially thrown open for business last year. Some ten cargoes of grain left that port, amounting in all to about two and a half million bushels. Now let us examine these shipments. Out of that two and a half million bushels, two million were shipped by the Continental Grain Company of New York and half a million by the Drteyfus Company, a French company also having its head office in New York. If there is so much merit in these American ports will my hon. friends kindly tell me why these American firms are shipping grain through Churchill? It cannot be patriotism; it cannot be mere sentiment; it must be a straight case of dollars and cents. I wish to say for the information of those hon. gentlemen that the Continental Grain Company saved four cents a bushel by shipping that grain through Churchill, in spite of the fact that they paid just twenty times higher marine insurance rates than the same grain would pay if shipped from Montreal. I Ihink that is something that is well worthy of consideration.
But that is not all. Last fall the Minister of Railways and Canals announced that the Churchill elevator would be available for winter storage. And it was filled to the roof. Once more I ask the question, by whom? By the Continental Grain Company of New York, for shipment this next summer. Surely there is something wrong with the western Canadian grain com,ponies, the wheat pool, the Grain Growers Limited, and these other people when they allow an American company to use that port, saving five or six or probably seven cents a bushel between now and the time the shipping season opens next spring. The Continental Grain Company will be able to undersell the Canadian dealers by five cents
a bushel on the Liverpool market. It is true that at the moment we are being penalized by iniquitous marine insurance rates. It is also true that the port of Montreal suffered from the same thing for many years. For a considerable time Montreal paid three and a half per cent; it was reduced to three per cent, then to two per cent, and it is now one-eighth of one per cent. But this reduction only came after many years had passed, and the necessary improvements had been made, of course, to that river route. In Churchill we are in the same position today as Montreal is as regards safety. There are no marine handicaps in Hudson bay or straits, in spite of the fact that we lost a boat this year, a boat that looked around two days before it found an iceberg.
Some hon. MEMBERS; Oh, oh.
Mr. STITT (Nelson); There is no question about that. That boat was deliberately sunk.

Mr. Chairman, there was considerable discussion this afternoon regarding the shipment of grain from Canada to Great Britain through American ports, but it seems to me that there is one point which has not been brought out very clearly. I think there is no doubt that under the present practice a large amount of grain is shipped from the head of the lakes to Buffalo and New York, particularly in the fall, and held in elevators there for shipment to any point where sales can be made, and at any time that sales can
1062	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
be made. This is particularly true of New York. Very often advantageous freight rates can be secured on wheat from New York to Liverpool and London because there are so many liners sailing from that port. It is rather significant that the freight rate from New York to Liverpool and London, as pointed out before, averaged two years ago four and a half cents a bushel, while the freight rate from New York to Glasgow was seven and a half cents, and the rate from New York to Antwerp and Dunkirk the same year was ten cents. I think that proves conclusively that it is the service available on the liners sailing out of New York to Liverpool and London which keeps those rates so low. I do not see how under the new arrangement wheat can be kept in New York elevators available for shipment on short notice on any liner sailing for Europe. The agent of a steamship company now goes to the exporter in New York and says something to this effect: We have space for fifty thousand bushels of wheat on a certain boat sailing the day after tomorrow. We will give you a very special rate; we will offer you four cents a bushel. That may 'be a saving of one-half or one cent or more over the usual rate, and will in many cases enable that exporter to make a sale to some person in the old country, a sale which he could not have made had he to pay the extra one or two cents a bushel freight. So far as I have been able to find out from listening to the discussion and reading the regulations it will not be possible to send half a million bushels of grain, for instance, from the head of the lakes for storage in New York elevators, and then be in a position to send it to the old country in ten or twelve different shipments going at different times and to ten or twelve different importers. If that cannot be done it will place an impediment in the way of the shipment of our grain through these channels and we will not be able to get the benefit of the low freight rates that we have enjoyed in the past. If this should be the case I think it is to be very much regretted, though of course I hope it will not turn out that way. So far I have been unable to see any way in which this can be handled. Once this agreement is put through in Great Britain-perhaps it is already in effect-I hope this government will do all they can to see that some regulations are brought in under which it will be possible to carry on this trade. Personally I do not know how it can be done, but perhaps the government can find some way of doing it.
Just before I sit down I should like to refer to what was said this afternoon with regard to shipping our grain through Saint

John and Halifax. I believe one hon. member said that the railways now granted a rate of six cents a bushel from Midland or other Georgian bay points to Halifax and Saint John. That distance must be at least nine hundred miles, and for the life of me I cannot see how our railways can afford to haul grain that distance for six cents a bushel. The distance from my shipping point in the west to Vancouver is about 800 miles; the rate is 12i cents per bushel, and we have been told repeatedly in this house that this rate is too low, that the railways are losing money. I do not think the railways are losing anything, but if they are hauling it at even the proper cost I do not see how they can afford to haul grain from Midland to Saint John for a rate fifty per cent lower. Surely we should be careful about forcing traffic into such uneconomic channels as this would appear to be. I think we should hesitate before we attempt to do the impossible. Someone said this afternoon that you cannot divert trade into new channels with a stroke of the pen. I would say that you can kill trade with a stroke of the pen, and I would suggest to members from the maritime provinces, with all due deference, that we are attempting the impossible when we say our railways should haul grain from Georgian bay points to Saint John and Halifax for six cents per bushel.
I think it is time wTe approached these problems from the economic point of view. Let us not try to do the impossible. The price of wheat is so low in western Canada, and the production of wheat is so important to Canada, as was pointed out by the Prime Minister this afternoon, that this parliament should do nothing, particularly at this time, W'hich will lower the net return to the wheat producer by so much as a fraction of a cent a bushel.

However, I will confine my remarks to as few sentences as possible.
In the first place, this government has nothing whatever to do with the fixing of the conditions under which goods are admitted to the United Kingdom.
In the second place, the regulation which has .been read into Hansard at least three times and referred to repeatedly during the debate is one which has been in force since about 1919. I am not quite sure of the precise date of its origin, but I have in my hand one regulation dated February 1, 1926, in which paragraph 12 appears as paragraph 13. I could read this paragraph again, but I do not see that anything would be gained by doing so. This regulation has been part of the regular law of the old country.
In the third place, let us remember this: Great Britain has passed these regulations for the control of business entering the country This particular one is applicable to Southern Rhodesia on fruits passing out at Beira; it is applicable to goods transshipped from New Zealand or South Africa; it is applicable to the transshipment of goods from the Straits Settlements at Hongkong, and it is applicable to goods going from Canada via New York Boston or any other American port. It is a regulation which has been in force and which has been operating successfully and satisfactorily. Those who argue the extreme on one side want everything to go through Canadian ports, while those who argue on

The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), and one or two others have been suggesting that there will be no shipping available at Canadian ports. I tell them now that the Cunard line are putting on a new service from Saint John and Halifax consisting of three sailings per week to London and Glasgow. Not only are these ships to be liners, but they are the vessels which have been going to New York. An official of the company advised me last night in my office that they were going to do this. Why are they doing it? Because we have entered into these agreements and they feel that the demand for shipping services from Canada will be sufficient to warrant this new service. Other steamship companies are doing the same thing.
Hon. members talk of these ports as though they were little by-ports. I was in Halifax a few weeks ago and I saw several ships from New York, Great Britain and other countries. These large ships constantly touch at this port, such ships as the Baltic and others. Some of the liners out of New York make a call at Halifax, which possesses a harbour unsurpassed by any other in this country, in-

eluding my own harbour of Vancouver. They can sail right into the harbour and up to the quayside within fifteen minutes. Elevator and other services are right at hand. Why should we decry our own ports when there is no need of doing so?
Saint John possesses marvelous facilities, and let me say that, yesterday I was advised on the very best of authority that, in spite of the fact that we had rebuilt the burned area last year-and by the way, that was a splendid achievement by the contractors, who did the job in four or five months-they expect that within a month or two there will not be sufficient space for the shipping coming into that harbour. But with all that, let us not forget that this has not been done at the sacrifice of any Canadian interest.
Let me say a word about the Buffalo situation. Some hon. gentleman-I have forgotten just who it was-said a moment ago that three-fifths of our grain goes out by Buffalo and that the benefit on all that is going to be lost to us. That is pure, unadulterated nonsense.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: That statement was not made by anyone.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It was made, because I heard it and I know what I am talking about. Let me explain how foolish such a statement is. In the first place, a substantial portion of the grain that goes out by Buffalo goes to the continent of Europe, and nothing in this agreement or the regulations interfere in that to the extent of a single bushel. In the second place, as regards that particular quantity which goes to the another country, a substantial portion will go, as it has always done, on through bill of lading as is provided for in the regulations. That is not touched. We have now narrowed the quantity down to a comparatively small balance. So my hon. friends, in raising these bogys are simply erecting hypothetical cases, imaginary grievances, something that is going to come with a big "if" in the future, instead of trying to look at this matter only in the interest of the west and of the east, in order that we may all pull together to make of Canada what it can be, one of the greatest countries on the face of the earth.
When I think of the old civilization down in the maritime provinces-and when I say "old civilization," I am speaking of it in contrast with the extreme north and west of this country, which are comparatively modern- when I think how the people down there stood behind the development of Canada, I feel it is about time we took an interest in their welfare. We need not sacrifice anything in so doing. Let us take at least a smiling interest in their welfare and see if we cannot help along business through those ports. I ask the same interest for the movement westward. In connection with this regulation, there is no need whatever to fear that any Canadian interest will be injured. On the other hand, it will probably greatly help Canadian interests and at the same time do no harm. Let us at least give it a chance.
When my hon. friends were speaking a moment ago they directed a question to me about the advantage of this six cent rate. It just struck me: What would they have said if this government, instead of securing a six cent rate, had said to the British government: Oh, well, we are not interested. The hon. member for Lisgar, who has spoken about the matter two or three times, asserts that the grain growers of western Canada say they do not want it. I can tell him that officials of the grain growers of western Canada, men much higher in their councils than he is, representative men, men who knew what they were talking about, men of standing, came to

Suppose we had taken the advice of the hon. member for Lisgar and one or two other hon. members opposite and said to the British government, as he tells us tonight we ought to have done: "We do not want this duty on wheat to apply to Canada at all." Let us view these agreements with a degree of common sense. What happened? I said this last night, but with apologies, Mr. Chairman, I shall reiterate it. We had a committee of all the dominions studying this question. I was chairman of the committee on cereals; the Minister of Mines was chairman of the committee on metals; Mr. Coates was chairman of the committee on dairy products. The cereal committee went into the whole question much as is expressed in the various agreements reached at the conference. Australia, South Africa and Canada were the countries chiefly affected. India was affected on some items only. Every one of them asked for a duty on wheat. New Zealand was not much interested. Then they went on to deal with the other items. I was delegated as chairman, together with Mr. Bruce, who accompanied me, to meet Mr. Chamberlain and Sir John Gilmour and discuss this question with them. The hon. member for Lisgar asks:	What
mysterious understandings were arrived at? There were no mysterious understandings; there was a frank conference between Mr. Chamberlain, Sir John Gilmour, Mr. Bruce and myself on this question, and we worked out the details as we have them before us. After that was done and the other committees reported, the whole matter was brought together into this composite form, and agreements with the various dominions drafted and

passed in the form in which they appear at the present time.
Let us, as I said a moment ago, get away from this idea of supposititious happenings in the future and try to face the facts that we have in these agreements advantages for Canada, for Australia and for South Africa. On the other hand, we have given the mother country advantages in this market. Let us try to view the situation from a business standpoint and give these agreements an opportunity to become effective. I can assure any hon. member opposite, as well as my hon. friends in the opposite corner to my right, who have been very reasonable in the matter, that after these agreements have been put into effect, should anything crop up that seems to be working harm to any Canadian interest, this government will certainly be glad to take the matter into consideration and do what is necessary to effect adjustment and improvement. That is the very reason we left the agreement in that form, so that consultations might be had for the removal of any difficulties or complaints.
I apologize to the committee for occupying so much time, but my hon. friend said that I was glued to my seat. I am not glued to my seat very often. My hon. friend takes great liberties in this house. The language he frequently uses is neither elevating to the house nor a credit to himself. But for long years we have known the hon. gentleman; we respect his age, we know his temperament, and let his observations pass. But when my hon. friend directs observations like that to me again I should like him to take at least some cognizance of the facts as they have been put before him in the speeches delivered by hon. members here this afternoon.

That article reads:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom undertake that the general ad valorem duty of ten per cent imposed by section 1 _ of the Import Duties Act, 1932, on the foreign goods specified in schedule C shall not be reduced except with the consent of His Majesty's government in Canada.
Article 22, states that the general duration of the agreement shall be five years. New or increased duties are to be levied on such commodities as wheat, rice, butter, cheese, eggs, condensed milk and various kinds of fruit, from other than dominion sources. Practically all these commodities form the food of the poor.

It would therefore be subject to article 1, and no margin of preference would be granted. Now the question is: Is any margin of preference guaranteed because there is a change from ad valorem to a specific duty or a change from one specific duty to another specific duty? The hon. member for Vancouver Centre says no, and he has this to support his contention, that the duties set out in schedule B are duties which are to be levied "in place of the duties, if any, now leviable"-notice, it is "now leviable." In other words, the object of

schedule B is not to place the duties therein mentioned in a different category from the hundred and one duties that are imposed upon the ordinary run of commodities entering the United Kingdom, and which are subject to article 1. It is simply to change the rate for the time being, and these duties are, as the article says, to take the place of duties now leviable. But the duties now leviable are, it is agreed by all, subject to change. That was settled last night by the admissions of the ministry. There is no margin of preference guaranteed on the hundred and one or thousand and one commodities on which Great Britain levies duties. Article 2 does not contain a single commodity upon which the duty remains as it is at the present time. If there were in the list duties which are the same as the duties now leviable, it would be a clear indication of the intention on the part of the persons entering into the agreement that that margin of preference was to be guaranteed for the five year period. That, I assume, is the basis of the argument which is being put forward in the British papers and to which my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre referred, and I suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it is not a frivolous argument. I hope and sincerely hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is right, and if there is any way of getting an agreement between the British government and this government as to the interpretation that is to be placed upon it, we should get it. The agreement is badly drafted as it stands now, when you take article 1 and article 2 together. maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
It must be remembered that schedules B and C are perhaps the most important part of this agreement. These are the items which were specifically selected for Canadian purposes and Canadian interests, and there can be no doubt whatever in my mind upon the point that has been raised. I quite see the reason for raising it, but there is no doubt in my mind as to what the acceptation of it is. In the first place we must bear in mind that this agreement is unquestionably one of good faith. It is not a forced contract in which there might be an attempt to escape from some of its provisions; on

United Kingdom
both sides it is an agreement in good faith. That is the first point to remember. In the second place the differentiation which the hon. member for Hants-Kings has pointed out between article 1 and article 2 is, I think, quite easily explained when one bears in mind that the main object of article 1 is the extension beyond November 15 of the provision of free entry. That is the major theme in that article, and article 2 deals specifically with what I might call the choice schedule of the whole agreement. Without stretching the reasonable legal interpretation, without stretching one's imagination or the language, and bearing in mind that the whole agreement is for a period of five years, and the fact that the British government's invitation to parliament to pass it was a serious undertaking, I submit that, article 2 providing as it does that the mother country will impose these duties, had the parliament of Great Britain not imposed them, the whole agreement would have fallen down. There is no question about that; the agreement would not have gone into force. But they undertook to do it; they presented it to parliament and passed the legislation and this now becomes the law of Great Britain and is enforceable for five years except with the consent of the dominion to vary it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: If that is the case-and I hope it is the proper construction of schedule B-then why have a different provision in article 3-in conjunction with schedule C-where it is specifically stated that the duties shall not be reduced except with the consent of His Majesty's government in Canada.

speechtext:

That was the reason why they were put in the form they are in article 3, in other words, the British did not wish to change the ten per cent rate on those articles. I may say that some suggestion was made that certain specific duties should be applied, but in the discussions it was thought to be not advisable. Therefore, they were left in the list with a ten per cent duty, but Great Britain undertakes that she will not reduce these articles below ten per cent. They are in contradistinction to the broad general list which is now outside these agreements altogether.

During the period of three years from the passing of this act or such further period as may be prescribed, any copper produced in any part of the British Empire but refined outside of the British Empire, being copper to which this subsection applies shall, subject to proof being given in the prescribed manner that it has been so produced and that it has been consigned from the country in which it was refined, be treated for the purposes of this section as if it had been consigned from a part of the British Empire.

I say the Liberal party did as much for the ports of Halifax and Saint John as any party in this country. We built the elevator at Halifax; we extended the facilities both at the deep water terminals and at the terminals up the harbour. Besides that, it was the Liberal party which arranged for the reduction in the rate on flour to compete with New York and shipped through Halifax and Saint John. The reason you will never get any great quantity of grain shipped through Halifax is this; these ships that come across the Atlantic do not turn there; on the western voyage they call only to land passengers and mail and then go on to New York. During the time they are turning in New York, some three or four days, they take the cargo on board, so that when they call at Halifax again on their eastbound trip they are delayed only an hour or so to take on mail and passengers. Until such time as this country has a population of from thirty to fifty millions, and until it changes its tariff policy, you will never get any great quantity of grain loaded at Halifax, because until such time as the ships load and unload their cargoes and turn at Halifax there will not be a very great movement of wheat from that port.

When this government came in it increased the duty on coal 50 per cent. When the Liberals came in in 1896 the duty was 60 cents a ton and they reduced it in two steps to 50 cents, but this government increased it to 75 cents per ton. That was the highest rate of duty ever placed on coal in Canada, so that the miners of Cape Breton realize that the pledges made to them by the present Prime Minister have been carried out as far as he was able to do so. Surely when a person is so obsessed with partisanship that he is not fair enough to give the present government credit for what it has done for the coal industry he is not in a position to pose in this house as an authority on the coal situation. It is true there has been a falling off in coal production in Nova Scotia, and I will tell you why. It is simply because the market for our coal in the industrial sections of Ontario and Quebec has been shot to pieces by this depression. That is the answer. As a result of that, and as a result also of the competition which our coal has to meet from oil, electricity and the development of hj'dro in many of the industries that previously used our coal, the market has diminished. The reason I was discussing the coal question was that no mention was made of coal in this agreement. I showed the committee that there had been a great falling off in the production of coal in Canada and practically no falling off in the production of coal in the United Kingdom. I admit that my hon. friend knows more about coal than I do, but figures do not lie, although liars may figure. They were not my figures; they were taken from the statistics as to the world's production of coal, and I do not think hon. members can insinuate that I am saying anything that is not correct. He should applaud me for the action I am taking, because he cannot very well get up and criticize the government for not having discussed this coal question at the conference. Instead of condemning me, he should praise me for standing up to argue in favour of the poor coal miner in Cape Breton South.
My hon. friend has said that this government has been very good to the miners in Nova Scotia, but its actions are no better than those of the previous government. I admit that both governments have given a subvention, but the late government did not do what this government did through its Minister of Mines (Mr. Gordon) in saying that because of the subvention they gave last year there would be a million tons more coal sold from the coal mines in Nova Scotia than in the previous year. My hon. friend said that because of the subvention given by this government 330,000 
tons moved this year from Nova Scotia to Ontario and Quebec, but the fact remains, which he admitted, that the sales of coal in Ontario and Quebec were very much below what they had been when the Liberal government was in power. He must not forget that the Liberal government also gave a subvention upon coal from Cape Breton and the west moving to Ontario and Quebec.
What I am complaining about is that in spite of the promise made in 1930 by the Prime Minister that he was going to see that the coal miners in Cape Breton obtained work, during the last two years nothing has been done to encourage the operation of the coal mines in the province of Nova Scotia.

Before the item passes I Should like to make a few observations with respect to the coal situation, especially with reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). I would not be making any observations were it not for his last remark, that I had made the statement that the subvention put on by this government would bring about an increase of a million tons in the production of the mines of Nova Scotia. I made no such statement either within or out of this house.
The problem which has confronted the government in connection with the coal situation has been complex and difficult. The desire was and is to have Canadian coal burned in Canada wherever it is economically possible and to support the coal mining industry throughout Canada in order that that industry might be preserved and the miners engaged therein be kept in fairly steady employment. I do not intend to make any statement with regard to the soundness of subventions, but the fact is that these subventions were commenced by the late government.
In connection with the prohibition of the importation of Russian coal, the motive which inspired this government to prohibit these importations was not a dislike for Russians as such. Russia was introducing into Canada a fuel to be sold at a cost below the possible cost of production in this country having regard to our standards of living and to the wages which we hoped to maintain to the labouring man in this country. This Russian coal was meeting competition only from American anthracite, a coal which we do not produce. There was great distress in the Welsh coal mines, which produce a kind of coal which is in my opinion better than the

United Kingdom
American anthracite. This coal was available to the Canadian market and, rightly or wrongly, the government decided to make this market available to the British coal miners, which has been done without any increase in price to the consumer. I contend that the prohibition of Russian anthracite to give favourable consideration to British coal was a very proper thing for this government to do.

speechtext: In regard to this article, I understand it was inserted in the agreement at the request of the British delegates who feared, because copper, zinc and lead were cartelized commodities, the prices of which were controlled by world-wide organizations, that grain might come into the same class because of the action of Canadian and Australian pools, and the British consumer might find himself at the mercy of certain powerful Canadian mergers, if one might call them such. Therefore they had that clause inserted to protect the British consumer. I do not see anywhere in the agreement any such clause that will protect the Canadian consumer. Everything coming into Canada appears to be introduced in the agreement with the idea of increasing the price. Is it possible that our government, in drafting the agreement, entirely lost sight of the Canadian consumer? I would like an answer from the minister.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The answer to the last part of the question is no.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: How' then are the Canadian consumers protected? They are not protected in the same way as is the British consumer. We have in this schedule articles the price of which is controlled by world wide organizations. It might easily happen, when we shut out competition from the outside world, that we shall find ourselves in the grip of a British monopoly, and yet our government has taken no steps to protect our consumers from such exploitation.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Our consumers are all protected by the statutory acts of Canada, the Combines Act and other acts.
Article 2 agreed to.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Might I ask
the right hon. the Prime Minister if as a matter of principle he would agree to a clause that no Canadian duties should be raised except upon the consent of the British government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I do not think the answer to a hypothetical question has anything to do with this case. This agreement is here, this paragraph is here, and the terms of the agreement are open to criticism. I do not propose to answer hypothetical questions.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I quite expected that my right hon. friend would not answer the question or even attempt to answer it. There is not a member of this parliament who would stand in his place and say that he would agree that any duty should not be raised or lowered in this country except with the consent of the British government, and yet we are being asked now to say that certain duties shall not be lowered in Great Britain except with the consent of the government of Canada.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: They have agreed to it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
They may have agreed to it, but I am speaking about what Canada is doing, not about what they are doing in Great Britain. I say I do not think this parliament should be asked to approve of anything in an agreement with respect to another country of the empire that this parliament itself would not be prepared to have put in an agreement respecting its own affairs. It establishes a precedent if it does nothing else, and an entirely wrong precedent. I cannot imagine anything better calculated to work mischief between the different parts of the British Empire than that one government should be permitted-I will go further and say that one parliament should be permitted -to do something within its jurisdiction only by consent of the government of some other part of the empire. It is impossible to think of any single thing that could be more at variance with the whole conception of selfgovernment, and all that relates to the autonomous rights of parliament and of a country than a condition which obliges the government of one part of the empire to maintain its tariff in any particular only by the consent of the government of another part of the empire. That is certainly substituting for the present ties of empire an economic tie that is in the nature of a fetter. It is not helping to make the relations, either economic or political, of the empire any closer. It is establishing the kind of thing that begets a sense of restraint, and once a sense of restraint is begotten arising from the interference by other governments with the government of one's own country, that moment trouble is certain to begin. I cannot conceive how any government of Canada could expect its parliament to support a course of action which brings us back to the days of the struggles of the thirteen colonies in the 18th century when they were asserting the right to regulate their tariffs to suit themselves. As hon. gentlemen well know it was an endeavour on the part of the government of one part of the empire as it was then to force the colonies to accept a duty on tea which led to the revolution and to the loss by Great Britain of her colonies- just that very sense of restraint that they were not free to do what they wished to do with regard to their own duties but had to act with the consent of a government across the sea. That is exactly the kind of thing this parliament is being asked to sanction at the present time in an agreement to which it is a party. Anyone who respects the right of self-government for himself should respect it equally for others, and any country that wants complete self-government and complete control of its fiscal policy should not be a party to an arrangement which is going to restrict the fiscal freedom of another country in however slight a manner. The principle involved, the precedent established, are all important. It is little wonder that an ex-member of the British government when he read that clause made the exclamation that so far as Great Britain herself is concerned " the day has come when we have not the status even of a dominion"; or words to that effect. ''Our status is something less than that of a dominion " were, I think his words. So far as dominion status is concerned, I wish to say that I believe it extends to complete freedom in all that pertains to the fiscal policy of a country. We in this parliament will claim that, and certainly those of us who belong to the Liberal party will be prepared to accord it to all other governments of the empire and will never ask anything to the contrary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is extraordinary that one with any experience should be guilty of the observations that have been made by the right hon. gentleman tonight. It is incredible, and when the public read them, when business men hear that in this house such statements were made by a reputable leader, they will not only be amazed but they will wonder, as they did the other evening, why they supported tying the dollar to the pound-Downing street and London are hereafter to fix the value of the dollar.
Here is a clause by which the British government said: This preference shall not fall below ten per cent unless Canada agrees, and there is a provision by which there shall be consultation between the two governments. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who is not in bis place, was sent to Ottawa as the special representative of Quebec to represent the lumber interests. He came to the conference for that purpose. The lumber interests suggested that it might be possible that this import rate of ten per cent be reduced. The same representations were made with respect to fish, because fish is regarded as very important, and also with respect to asbestos, zinc and lead. The British government said: We certainly will agree to a provision in this agreement that the duty shall not be less than ten per cent unless you agree. And according to the right hon. gentleman this is now a constitutional problem which is going to wreck the whole sanctity of the ark of the covenant and Britain is about to abdicate her position as a great power. Suppose the right hon. gentleman begins to think for once about his own country. Suppose he abandons this solicitude for other countries and begins to think about his own. Suppose he begins to think whether it was wise or not that there should be adequate safeguards that the duty on lumber should not go below ten per cent. Suppose he begins to think of the interests also of the producers of lead, zinc and asbestos, and of fish from the sea.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It does not mean anything at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: All that this does is to say that there shall be no reduction of that ten per cent preference unless both parties agree to it. I am glad that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough says that it means nothing at all, because his leader has said that it means a very great deal. One thinks that it is going to wreck the empire, and the other that it does not mean anything at all.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: He is talking about the constitutional question; and I am talking about the practical question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: It is wrecking the empire to one, and to the other it is quite all right; it means nothing. Between those two extremes you perhaps can get the moderate view.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: You are the happy medium.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Exactly. The phraseology was acceptable to the British government, as I have said; that with respect to these matters there should be no change without the agreement of both parties to the contract. It could have been put in this way: We agree to a ten per cent preference and it shall not be changed without the consent of both parties to the agreement. To the right hon. gentleman, of course, it is a constitutional question, wrecking the constitutional rights and privileges of all the people.
